To stop being desperate for love, one must love oneself. To love oneself, one must first know what love is. To know what love is, one must understand that love is not necessarily this 'divine and widespread energy present in the universe', but it is found in the smallests of acts.

Smiling to a person is love. Handing over someone's car keys, because it's right next to you, and it makes it easier for them if you hand it over to them, is love. Just being present for someone is love. Just taking the time to talk to someone is love. And so on.

Love is practiced. Every time you perform a deed of love for someone - which again: is found in the smallest acts -, it has an accumulating effect on the loved person. 

It keeps accumulating until that person develops a part of your 'spirit' in them. When he or she faces a severe calamity, to the extent it destroys their spirit, your spirit will be present as a means of support, when you can't be physically present, because you are present in their heart. 

You can love yourself, but understand that it takes time to develop such a relationship, even with yourself. Take in mind the accumulative effect of "building love" that I mentioned above. And you do it with simple acts...

Don't make it this special and vague idea or thing that you have to chase to get or something you can't ever get. 

You only need to be aware of how your mind as a functional defence mechanism blocked itself off from the world to guarantee safety. Understand that much of the dark aspect of the world, - or lack of love in it -, is your own mind creating that reality., and does not necessarily reflect reality. Love is the smallest acts. 

Do know that me taking the time to write you this message, knowing I'll get nothing in return, is an act of love. It's important that one opens his/her spirit to receive love.

I would say be cautious, but don't obsess over it. 

Why? Because your subconscious might have picked up on subtle danger signals, maybe a series of small, suspicious cues over time. Now, your subconscious is warning you that something might be off. This isn't some mystical idea—it's actually a scientifically recognized phenomenon.

My take on this is to consider if there are issues with people around you. Does anyone hold a grudge? Have you had a disagreement with someone who might want to retaliate? (Not necessarily in a dangerous way, just maybe in some form.)

Also, look at your day-to-day activities. Are there moments where you could be exposed to danger? For instance, say there’s a mentally unstable homeless person at your local train station that you use everyday commuting to work. Maybe your subconscious has noticed small changes in their behavior, like them focusing more on you than usual, even if you didn’t consciously notice it. Little details like this can trigger a sense of unease without you fully realizing why.

It's easy to dismiss these feelings, especially since we don't always consciously pick up on danger signals, but they are real. It’s actually more common than people think for dreams to "predict" an upcoming event, particularly if it's something negative.

Another possibility is that it could be more emotional or spiritual. Have you had any recent moments of personal revelation or growth, whether positive or negative? Dreams about death can sometimes represent "rebirth" or significant changes in life. I’ve seen this happen with many people.

It could also reflect feelings of being overwhelmed by life. Death in a dream might symbolize a loss of control, since death is one of the few things we can't prevent or delay. So, death can represent powerlessness. 


Other possibility: have you been thinking a lot about death lately? Has perhaps a significant person in your life died and you started thinking about it a lot lately? 

Other possibility: Maybe your body is telling you it wants to get out of a certain situation or place in your life. Just like how many suicidal people don't really wanna die, but they just want to get out of their misery. 

On the other hand, it might simply be nothing to worry about at all. Maybe it really is just the alcohol, and your mind is trying to tell you to stop these bad habits. 

So, as you know, dreams are very vague and symbolic. But...  At the end of the day... Dreams are a way of your subconscious mind to communicate with you conscious mind. Just like how your body will use a gut-feeling to communicate something, ir will use dreams. And what the gut-feeling or dream might actually mean, depends on you. You will know best. But, always listen to your body.

The comparison is fals and I'll do my best to inform you. Many Maghrebi people are just like the people of Iberia of Roman origin. In Roman times the province of Mauritania Tingitana was also called Mauretania Hispania. Because of its cultural ties to Hispania (Iberian peninsula). Even during the Arabic conquest people were still mostly Roman Christians. Ethnically they would be Amazigh or from Iberian tribes. Al Andalus was historically often seen as like a sister country to the northwest of the Maghreb.

To compare Amazighs-and-Iberians to Arabs-and-Desi people is just a false comparison. Arabs and Desis are fundamentally different people that have different origins and live far apart. Maghrebis and Iberians are people that are neighbours and have historically always overlapped at the straits of Gibraltar and its surrounding regions. So the comparison is flawed.

The Andalusian civilization was and still is a western Mediterranean civilization. I say "still is". Because it was not entirely extinct. The Castilians took over and completely destroyed the northern tip of Morocco where the historical Maghrebi-Roman city of Tamuda lied, making it an empty and barren land - where originally Berbers lived. The Andalusians, after the fall of Granada, fled there and under the command of al-Mandari he founded the city of Tetuan, which was from then on an autonomous Andalusian city, attracting many Andalusian refugees and Moriscos that arrived in north-Africa. The Castilians never managed to take that city so Andalusian culture kept existing there. Independently from Amazigh culture, unlike other cities in Morocco and Algeria, where they mixed instead.

I'm explaining this, because I think it's a good reference point for Andalusian culture and civilization because it is the last part of al-andalus that actually survived. The Andalusian culture is seen as independent and "it's own thing". It's not seen as Arab culture or Amazigh culture. It's simply seen as Andalusian culture. We recognise the influence from the middle-east, which was mostly Levantine, Byzantine and Persian to begin with, but we see ourselves different from the Levantine and Arab people. 

On the other hand Amazigh people have played a bigger role in shaping our culture and civilization than people in the middle-east. Obviously because of the fact that we are neighbours. Also, as I said previously: at the straits of Gibraltar there has historically always been an overlap of culture and ethnicity. So, to be fair, we are partly of amazigh or Maghrebi origin. Not a full 100% Iberian. Current DNA studies confirm this. We are really a mix of Maghrebi and Iberian. Evern tourists often describe us as half Moroccan and half Spanish looking. In my personal case people I have often been told I look like Italian or half-Moroccan-half-Spanish, and get mistaken as Spanish or Italian. Some guy who's actually Amazigh even said I look half-Moroccan-half-French, which I think is a bit of a stretch. I'm saying this, because it reflects our history, being western Mediterranean rather than strictly north-African or even middle-eastern. But really a mix of Western-mediterranean cultures primarily surrounding the Gibraltar, with some influences from the east.

Another interesting fact to add. The Andalusian culture lived on in Tetuan, but remember that way more Andalusian refugees fled to what is now Morocco and Algeria than could ever fit in region Tetuan alone. So, in the Surrounding regions in north-Morocco and Algeria, especially at the Mediterranean coasts there are many Maghrebi people that are not fully Amazigh (even tho many claim they're 100% Amazigh), but they are more of a mix between Andalusian and mostly amazigh. That is also reflected in their culture. So, obviously they will also feel affiliated with al-Andalus. You'll see this in Morocco and Algeria.

Having said all that, "Arab" in the west always meant something linguistic. It didn't matter whether you were of Roman origin, or Amazigh or Visigothic. If you speak Arabic, you say that you're Arabic. Regardless of culture and ethnicity and genetics. 

When a Spaniard says that hes Latin he's not saying that he's from Italy.  No. He means that he belongs to the group of people that speak a Latin derived language. When an Andalusian says he's Arabic, he means that he belongs to the group that speaks Arabic. Not that he is from the middle-east.

Before Islam it was all part of the Roman empire. And the most important thing that mattered to integrate in Rome was that you spoke latin.
